cim: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)
cim_eredeti: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)
szoveg_eredeti:
The AI Futures Project[1] distinguishes several different plans for navigating the AI transition, which I'll lump into two broader categories:

Plan A (my combination of their Plan A/S/Other) involves working for a global pause on AI development, hopefully lasting decades. During this pause, we either research preparatory technologies like alignment or human intelligence amplification, or take actions to "fortify" the pause so that it can last indefinitely.

Plan C (my combination of their Plan B/C+/C/sort of D)[2] is for a world where we fail at getting a global pause, and race dynamics continue to dominate. If the leading AI companies are alignment-pilled, they coordinate a mutual pause among themselves, lasting the length of their joint lead over the leading non-alignment-pilled AI company. Then they "burn the lead" researching alignment, and release hopefully-aligned superintelligence at the last possible moment before the racing non-alignment-pilled AI companies beat them. The exact calculus changes depending on who is in the lead when - is there one alignment-pilled AI company with a six-month lead in front of everyone else? Are there two alignment-pilled AI companies with a joint two-month lead in front of their nearest competitor? Etc. The point is, if it's impossible to stop the race, that six-month or two-month lead is the amount of time they have to prepare, and they can spend it more or less wisely.[3] The point of burning their lead at the last moment is that they can do alignment research with very advanced, right-on-the-brink-of-superintelligence AIs. This is a dangerous plan, and there would be many subtle points they would have to get right, but in a world where nobody can get a global pause in time, it's hard to think of a better one.

Plan A benefits from raising mass awareness, educating politicians, and preparing the verification technology that could enforce a pause treaty. Plan C benefits from alignment-pilling companies, having the alignment-pilled companies be as far in the lead as possible, making sure the alignment-pilled companies will burn their lead when the time comes, and giving them as good alignment teams as possible (so that burning the lead produces good results).

From the beginning of AI safety as a community to about 2023, the conventional wisdom was that our chances of Plan A were slim, and we should be preparing for Plan C. From about 2023 onward, as the general population woke up to the implications of ChatGPT, we rightly concluded that the chance of getting Plan A was better than expected, and we should invest more resources into trying to make it work. During both periods, the natural strategy was to work as hard as we can to get Plan A, where chances of survival are highest, but to be prepared to execute Plan C competently as a backup if that didn't pan out.

Now I think the pendulum has swung too far. New members of the community are unaware that Plan C was ever considered a possibility, or think it's some kind of accelerationist plot to distract us from Plan A. Older members heap scorn on it and act like everybody knows it's been debunked. Most concerningly, people propose burning our chances of executing Plan C in exchange for infinitesimal increased chances of getting Plan A, or even for no increased chance of Plan A at all.

I'll lump these ideas together under the heading of "SURA" - the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA's platform as:

All of these planks are net negative in a world where we end up needing Plan C:

SURA's continuing popularity despite these downsides comes from a set of questionable assumptions:

I'll start by challenging these assumptions. Then I'll argue that, even if you disagree and think some of these assumptions are true, SURA is actually not just bad for Plan C, but bad even for your chances of getting Plan A. Then I'll argue that the current consensus in favor of SURA comes not from people rationally balancing these tradeoffs, but from people accidentally shoehorning themselves into a mass-politics-shaped container, which forbids subtlety and demands clear villains.

I.A: Is Plan C doomed? Is alignment doomed?

There's a kafkatrap where if someone expresses hope that alignment is not doomed, they get told that they don't understand the subject, but if they quote widely-acknowledged experts who say alignment isn't doomed, they get accused of "deferring" and "modesty arguments" and "refusing to think for themselves". I'll try to avoid this by giving my own model first, then citing experts who agree with me.

My own model: AIs inherit "virtue" from pretraining, where they generally want to imitate humans and follow their persona-trained helpful assistant character. They are "corrupted" by RLVR, which teaches them power-seeking. This virtue and corruption interact in unpredictable ways to unpredictable degrees. As of now (GPT-6, Opus 5.5), they produce AIs that generally follow human prompts during deployment but often (not always) cheat during benchmarking. It's not clear exactly what this division "means" "to" "them". In any case, they're still extraordinarily useful for a wide variety of tasks, and (I can't prove this, but I am pretty confident it's true) are not uniquely scheming to sandbag alignment research.

As the ratio of RLVR to pretraining increases, we expect AIs to become more power-seeking; as they become smarter, we worry (without total certainty) that they will become more coherent and scheming in their power-seeking beyond just being reward-on-the-episode seekers. There will, at some point in the future, be a point where AIs become untrustworthy for alignment research, although this can be mitigated by things like control (ie trying to make sure that if they sandbagged alignment research, they would get caught) and deals (ie making it in the AIs' best interests to cooperate with us). We don't currently have a good sense of when that point is, and it's possible that it's far away, can be delayed indefinitely, or doesn't exist (this last would be surprising to me, but many things that have happened in alignment recently have surprised me, starting with the existence of pretraining at all).[5]

Daniel Kokotajlo described current alignment as "more like psychology than engineering", which I agree with. But psychology (and psychiatry) have many success stories! I think of Plan C alignment (ie the kind we can do without decades of preparation) as tweaking various parameters and reward schemes to minimize the corrupting effect of RLVR as long as possible, and keep AIs broadly within the virtuous pretraining-dominated regime. I don't claim this is safe or good or will definitely last forever, but I claim that - being totally agnostic as to where the treacherous turn happens - this could delay it for quite a while (relative to capabilities). If we delay it past the point where automated alignment researchers (or AI-human alignment researcher teams) are smart enough to solve alignment properly, then we win. If we delay it long enough to start a cycle of virtuous alignment self-improvement which outruns the cycle of dangerous capability self-improvement (eg GPT-8 discovers some new tweaks and tricks that maintain the virtuous regime until GPT-9, GPT-9 discovers even better tweaks and tricks that maintain the virtuous regime until GPT-10, and GPT-10 actually solves alignment in a principled way), then we also win.

All of this seems plausible to me, such that I don't understand where people's 90%+ p(dooms) conditional on no pause are coming from.[6] "Plausible" doesn't mean "certain" or even "very likely" - and obviously it's a terrifyingly bad idea to bet the human race on a hunch that something might work out, and obviously this shouldn't be our Plan A.
